title: Campus Placement Drive Process & Preparation Strategy
content:
A standard Tier-1 and Tier-2 engineering campus placement drive is organized into 5 sequential stages:
1. Aptitude & Technical MCQs: 45-60 minutes evaluating quantitative ability, logical reasoning, verbal ability, and core CS MCQs (C/C++ output, pointers, OS scheduling, SQL queries, time complexity analysis).
2. Online Algorithmic Assessment (OA): 60-90 minutes containing 2-3 algorithmic problems on platforms like HackerRank, HackerEarth, Mettl, or Codility. Passing criteria typically requires solving 80%+ test cases with optimal time and space complexity.
3. Technical Interview Round 1 (DSA & Coding): 45-60 minutes live coding round focusing on Arrays, Strings, Trees, Linked Lists, Stack/Queue, and Recursion. Expect deep questions on edge cases and optimal big-O complexity.
4. Technical Interview Round 2 (Projects & Core CS): 45-60 minutes evaluating your resume projects in depth (architecture, technical decisions, challenges faced, database schema) along with Core CS fundamentals (OS, DBMS, Computer Networks, OOP).
5. HR / Fitment Round: 20-30 minutes evaluating communication skills, cultural adaptability, handling workplace conflict, career ambitions, and company background research.
Key Strategy: Maintain a consistent daily DSA problem habit 3-4 months prior to placement season and build 2 substantial full-stack or system projects with deployed live links.

title: Operating Systems (OS) Core Fundamentals for Tech Interviews
content:
Crucial Operating System topics asked frequently in technical interviews:
1. Process vs Thread: A process is an executing program instance with its own independent address space, PCB, and file descriptors. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process sharing the same address space, heap, and open files, but having its own private stack and registers. Context switching between threads is significantly faster than between processes.
2. Concurrency & Synchronization: Race conditions occur when multiple threads read/write shared mutable state without synchronization. Mitigated using Mutex (binary locking) and Semaphores (counting resource access). Critical section problem is solved using Dijkstra's algorithm, Peterson's algorithm, or hardware atomic operations (Compare-And-Swap).
3. Deadlocks: A state where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for another resource held by someone else. Four Coffman Conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Prevented via Resource Ordering or Banker's Algorithm (safe state avoidance).
4. Memory Management & Paging: Virtual memory decouples logical address space from physical RAM using page tables and MMU (Memory Management Unit). Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into page frames. Page faults happen when a requested page is not in physical memory, requiring a page replacement policy like LRU, FIFO, or Optimal.

title: Database Management Systems (DBMS) & SQL Interview Concepts
content:
Master these Database concepts for placement and SDE interview rounds:
1. ACID Properties: Atomicity (all-or-nothing execution), Consistency (database transitions between valid schema-conforming states), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute independently without interference, configured via isolation levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable), Durability (committed changes persist even upon hardware crashes via Write-Ahead Logging / WAL).
2. Database Normalization: Systematic decomposition of tables to minimize redundancy and eliminate insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. Key forms: 1NF (atomic values, no repeating groups), 2NF (1NF + no partial dependency on composite key), 3NF (2NF + no transitive dependencies), BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key).
3. Indexing Internals: Indices accelerate data retrieval at the cost of slower writes and additional disk storage. Relational databases predominantly use B+ Trees because leaf nodes are linked sequentially for efficient range scans and tree depth is shallow (logarithmic search). Clustered Index dictates physical sorting of rows (one per table, usually Primary Key); Non-Clustered Index stores a separate pointer structure referencing data rows.
4. SQL Joins vs Subqueries: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching right rows (NULL otherwise). Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK) are critical for complex analytics queries.
5. SQL vs NoSQL: SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL) provides strict schemas, ACID compliance, and relational integrity suited for financial transactions and structured entities. NoSQL (MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra) offers schema flexibility, horizontal scaling (sharding), and high throughput for semi-structured documents, caching, and time-series streams.

title: Computer Networks (CN) Interview Preparation Guide
content:
Essential Computer Networks concepts tested in campus and SDE interviews:
1. OSI Model 7 Layers: Physical (bits, cables), Data Link (frames, MAC addresses, Ethernet), Network (packets, IP routing, ICMP), Transport (segments, TCP/UDP port multiplexing), Session (session management), Presentation (encryption, compression, SSL/TLS), Application (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP).
2. TCP vs UDP: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented, reliable, guarantees in-order segment delivery, performs flow control (sliding window) and congestion control (Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance). UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless, lightweight, unreliable, low-overhead, ideal for real-time gaming, video streaming (WebRTC), and DNS lookups.
3. TCP 3-Way Handshake: Connection establishment: SYN (client to server with seq x) -> SYN-ACK (server responds with ACK x+1 and seq y) -> ACK (client sends ACK y+1). Teardown uses a 4-way FIN/ACK handshake.
4. What happens when you type a URL in your browser: (a) Browser checks local cache (browser, OS, router, ISP DNS cache). (b) If not found, recursive DNS resolution asks Root Server, TLD Server (.com), and Authoritative Nameserver to get IP address. (c) Browser initiates TCP 3-way handshake with server IP on port 80/443. (d) For HTTPS, TLS handshake negotiates encryption cipher and exchanges certificates. (e) Browser sends HTTP GET request. (f) Web server processes request and returns HTTP response (HTML, CSS, JS). (g) Browser engine parses DOM, constructs render tree, and paints the webpage.

title: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) & SOLID Principles
content:
Object-Oriented Programming and Software Design core interview expectations:
1. Four Pillars of OOP: 
   - Encapsulation: Bundling data and methods into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access via access specifiers (private, protected, public).
   - Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation complexity and exposing only essential interfaces via abstract classes and interfaces.
   - Inheritance: Mechanism where a child class acquires properties and behaviors from a parent class, promoting code reusability.
   - Polymorphism: Ability to take multiple forms. Compile-time polymorphism (Method Overloading) vs Runtime polymorphism (Method Overriding using virtual functions or dynamic dispatch).
2. SOLID Principles:
   - Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): A class should have only one reason to change.
   - Open/Closed Principle (OCP): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.
   - Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking application correctness.
   - Interface Segregation Principle (ISP): Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces they do not use.
   - Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend upon abstractions.
3. Common Design Patterns:
   - Creational: Singleton (single instance), Factory Pattern (decoupled instantiation), Builder (step-by-step object construction).
   - Structural: Adapter (interface conversion), Decorator (dynamic feature wrapping).
   - Behavioral: Observer (event pub/sub), Strategy (interchangeable algorithms).

title: Off-Campus Job Hunting & Referral Strategy
content:
Proven systematic methodology to land off-campus interviews at top product companies:
1. Targeted Resume Tailoring: Ensure ATS compliance with a single-column layout, clear action verbs, and quantifiable bullet points following Google's formula: 'Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y] by doing [Z]'.
2. The Referral Funnel: Applying through public job portals has less than 2-5% response rate. Referrals increase interview callback odds by 5x-10x. Identify engineers at target companies on LinkedIn who are alumni of your college or active in the same tech stack.
3. Crafting the Perfect Outreach Message: Keep it under 100 words. (a) Friendly greeting acknowledging their work. (b) 2-sentence summary of your profile, top tech stack, and key achievement (e.g., 'LeetCode 1900+ rating, built full-stack distributed payment app'). (c) The specific Job ID / URL you qualify for. (d) A link to your polished PDF resume and GitHub portfolio. Never say just 'Hi sir please refer me'.
4. Open Source & Hackathons: Participating in Smart India Hackathon (SIH), Google Summer of Code (GSoC), or contributing PRs to popular open-source repositories provides immediate real-world engineering credibility that distinguishes your profile from thousands of generic resumes.
